screens.title: Upgradeable Smart Contracts & Proxy Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts on Ethereum are immutable by design. That immutability gives strong guarantees, but it also raises a practical problem: real software needs fixes and new features. In this lesson you’ll learn why upgradeable contracts exist, how the EVM opcode delegatecall makes them possible, and two widely used proxy patterns — Transparent Proxy and UUPS. You’ll also see a full code walkthrough of a simple proxy plus a practical upgrade flow using OpenZeppelin’s UUPS plugins. By the end you will be able to explain how a proxy preserves state while swapping implementation logic, why storage layout matters, how an initializer replaces a constructor, and where common pitfalls lie. A concrete example in this chapter shows deploying a token using UUPS, then upgrading it to add a burn function while keeping balances intact. Keep in mind a common misconception: upgradeability does not remove immutability of on-chain history, it simply separates state and logic so logic can evolve. As you proceed, notice how delegatecall preserves msg. sender, msg. value, and the proxy’s storage — that is the core insight that enables safe, stateful upgrades.

screens.title: Immutability and the Upgradeability Problem
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum smart contracts are immutable once deployed. That immutability means the bytecode at an address cannot be altered, which preserves trust. However, immutability also prevents bug fixes and feature additions in the deployed code. Imagine a token contract with a bug in its transfer logic discovered after months of use. Redeploying a new contract would mean migrating all balances and convincing users to move to a new address — a costly and error-prone process. Upgradeable contracts solve this by separating state and logic: a proxy holds the state and user-facing address, while the logic lives in separate implementation contracts that the proxy can point to. The central claim is this: by using a forwarding mechanism that runs implementation code in the proxy’s storage, we can change behavior without changing state or address. A common misconception is thinking upgrades change historical transactions; they do not. The chain’s history remains intact. What changes is the active logic that handles new calls. The practical significance is large: projects can fix critical bugs, patch vulnerabilities, or add features while preserving on-chain data. Consider a simple token: with a proxy you can add a burn function later without moving balances. To make this safe, we must understand how forwarding works and what can go wrong with storage layout.

keyIdea.title: Why upgradeability
keyIdea.text: Separate state from logic so you can improve or fix on-chain behavior without migrating user data or changing the contract address.

content.html:
Core Concept

Definition

Immutability prevents changes to deployed contract code. Upgradeability keeps state stable while swapping logic.

Concrete example
A deployed token with stored balances can receive a new implementation that adds a burn function while balances remain in the proxy.
Misconception
Upgrading logic does not rewrite past transactions or on-chain history; it only changes the active code that processes new calls.
Visual: state vs logic
State
Balances, allowances, configuration stored in the proxy contract's storage slots.
Logic
Implementation contracts contain business logic that can be replaced if stored data layout is preserved.
Key takeaway
Upgradeability trades a single immutable code object for a controlled indirection that keeps storage stable while allowing logic evolution.

screens.title: delegatecall — the low-level mechanism
screens.narratorSegment: delegatecall is the EVM opcode that makes proxy-based upgrades possible. Unlike a normal external call which uses the callee’s storage and context, delegatecall executes the code of a target contract while keeping the storage, msg. sender, and msg. value of the calling contract. Practically, this means the proxy forwards the calldata to the implementation and executes that implementation's code against the proxy’s storage layout. A clear example: if an implementation’s increment function increments a storage slot named value, using delegatecall causes that slot in the proxy to change. A common misconception is treating delegatecall like a message that simply runs code elsewhere; instead it effectively borrows the implementation’s code and operates directly on the proxy’s state. This behavior is powerful but dangerous: bugs in implementation code write directly into the proxy's storage. Because delegatecall preserves msg. sender, access control checks in the implementation will see the original caller rather than the proxy, which is usually desired. When designing proxies, always ensure the proxy correctly forwards calls and returns data and that the implementation functions are written with the assumption they operate on the proxy state. As you move to code examples, keep this operational model in mind — it explains storage collisions and why initializers must be called through the proxy.

keyIdea.title: delegatecall essence
keyIdea.text: delegatecall runs target code with the calling contract’s storage and caller context, enabling logic to operate on proxy-held state.

content.html:
Definition

What delegatecall does

  • Executes code of the implementation contract.
  • Uses the proxy’s storage, keeping state persistent across upgrades.
  • Preserves msg.sender and msg.value so access checks see the original caller.
Concrete example
An implementation increment function that increases a value variable will change the proxy’s storage slot for value when invoked through delegatecall.
Pitfall
Because the implementation writes into the proxy’s storage, variable ordering must remain consistent across upgrades to avoid collisions.
Call flow visual
User
Sends tx to proxy address with calldata for a function.
Proxy
Forwards calldata with delegatecall to implementation; retains storage and msg.sender.
Implementation
Runs logic using proxy’s storage and returns result to proxy which returns to user.
Check your understanding
Why must initializers be called through the proxy rather than on the implementation contract directly? Because the constructor is not executed in proxy context; only calls executed through delegatecall affect proxy storage.

screens.title: Proxy and Implementation Roles
screens.narratorSegment: A proxy is minimal by design: it holds state variables and a pointer to the current implementation address, and it forwards all external calls to that implementation via delegatecall. The implementation contract contains business logic and assumes storage exists in the calling context. This separation gives two distinct responsibilities. The proxy is responsible for state persistence and upgradeability mechanics — storing the implementation pointer and enforcing who can change it. The implementation focuses on behavior: token transfers, business rules, and access checks. This division has consequences. For example, any storage layout declared in the implementation must match what the proxy expects at the same slots. Also, access control in the implementation should operate against msg. sender as seen through delegatecall, which means the implementation can enforce permissions that reference the original caller. The Transparent Proxy pattern adds admin handling in the proxy itself, allowing the admin to make management calls that are not forwarded. UUPS moves upgrade authorization into the implementation. When designing your system, think of the proxy as a stable envelope for evolving logic. A helpful analogy is a building with fixed wiring (state) and replaceable appliances (logic): you swap appliances without rewiring the house. What can go wrong? If upgrade authority is misconfigured or storage layouts differ between versions, you risk breaking the contract and corrupting user data.

keyIdea.title: Architecture insight
keyIdea.text: Proxy = storage and forwarding; Implementation = logic executed with proxy storage via delegatecall; both must be designed to match storage layout and trust boundaries.

content.html:
Architecture

Proxy responsibilities

  • Store persistent state (balances, config).
  • Keep a pointer to the implementation address.
  • Forward calls using delegatecall and return results.

Implementation responsibilities

  • Contain business logic: transfers, minting, and application rules.
  • Assume it operates on proxy storage layout when executed via delegatecall.
  • Optionally include upgrade authorization hooks for UUPS.
Example call path
User -> proxy address; proxy delegatecalls implementation; implementation runs logic that modifies proxy storage; proxy returns result. Because delegatecall preserves msg.sender, the implementation sees the user as the caller.
Analogy
Think of the proxy as a safe deposit box holding account data, and implementation contracts as different vault managers whose rules operate on the same contents.
Key Takeaway

Clear separation of state and logic is flexible but requires strict alignment of storage layout and upgrade authority rules.

screens.title: Transparent Proxy vs UUPS
screens.narratorSegment: Two prominent proxy patterns are the Transparent Proxy and UUPS. The Transparent Proxy places upgrade logic in the proxy contract itself and distinguishes calls from the admin and regular users. If the caller is the admin and the function matches a proxy-defined admin function, the proxy performs management actions; otherwise it delegatecalls to the implementation. This avoids accidental interception of admin functions by users, but introduces a limitation: the admin cannot call implementation functions that share signatures with the proxy. UUPS moves the upgrade logic into the implementation. The proxy becomes minimal — it only forwards calls and stores the implementation pointer. The implementation exposes functions like _authorizeUpgrade, and upgrade execution happens within the implementation contract. UUPS is more gas-efficient because the proxy is small, and it avoids the Transparent Proxy's signature clash. However, UUPS requires that every new implementation includes proper upgrade hooks; forgetting to include them makes the contract un-upgradeable. A practical contrast: Transparent Proxy centralizes upgrade authority into the proxy, which can be simpler to reason about in some governance models, while UUPS gives implementations control and relies on developer discipline. Which you choose depends on desired gas profile, governance model, and whether you want upgrade checks centralized or bundled with logic.

keyIdea.title: Pattern trade-off
keyIdea.text: Transparent Proxy centralizes admin logic in the proxy; UUPS moves upgrade hooks into the implementation for smaller proxies and lower gas, but requires consistent upgrade code in each implementation.

content.html:
Comparison
Transparent Proxy
  • Proxy contains admin and upgrade logic.
  • Proxy distinguishes admin calls from user calls to avoid conflicts.
  • Admin cannot call implementation functions with same signature as proxy functions.
UUPS
  • Proxy is minimal: only forwarding logic and implementation pointer.
  • Implementation contains _authorizeUpgrade and upgrade functions.
  • Gas-efficient, but each implementation must include upgrade hooks or upgrades are impossible.

Concrete scenario

If you expect frequent upgrades and want low per-call gas cost, UUPS is attractive because the proxy adds minimal overhead. If you prefer centralizing upgrade control and making the proxy explicitly handle admin flows, Transparent Proxy may be clearer. In both cases, protect upgrade authority and test storage compatibility before upgrading.
Common mistake
With UUPS, forgetting to include _authorizeUpgrade in a new implementation will lock the system and prevent future upgrades. With Transparent Proxy, misplacing admin calls can intercept expected implementation behavior.

screens.title: Basic Proxy Example
screens.narratorSegment: Looking at a minimal proxy example helps cement how forwarding and upgrade work. In the example proxy, the contract stores an implementation address and an admin address. An upgradeTo function lets the admin set a new implementation address with an authorization check. The fallback function uses delegatecall with the incoming msg. data, then returns the implementation result using inline assembly. This pattern means functions not defined on the proxy will be handled by delegatecall and executed against the proxy’s storage. The important operational detail is that the implementation’s constructor is never run in proxy context. Instead, state initialization must happen through an initializer function called via the proxy after deployment. A misconception to avoid: calling initialize on the implementation contract directly will set values in the implementation’s storage, not the proxy’s. Always call initialize through the proxy address. The code walkthrough in the content shows both a simple implementation contract with a value variable and the MyProxy contract with upgrade and fallback logic. Read the code to see where delegatecall is used and where admin checks guard upgrades. After you review the code, consider how you would add a reentrancy guard or access control while preserving storage layout.

keyIdea.title: Proxy mechanics
keyIdea.text: The fallback delegatecall forwards execution to an implementation; upgradeTo changes the implementation pointer under admin control. Initialization must run through the proxy.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Implementation example (logic)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyLogicV1 {
  uint256 public value;

  function initialize(uint256 _initialValue) public {
    require(value == 0, "Already initialized");
    value = _initialValue;
  }

  function increment() public {
    value++;
  }

  function getVersion() public pure returns (string memory) {
    return "MyLogicV1";
  }
}
Proxy example (forwarding)
contract MyProxy {
  address public implementation;
  address public admin;

  constructor(address _implementation) {
    implementation = _implementation;
    admin = msg.sender;
  }

  function upgradeTo(address _newImplementation) public {
    require(msg.sender == admin, "Not authorized");
    implementation = _newImplementation;
  }

  fallback() external payable {
    (bool success, bytes memory result) = implementation.delegatecall(msg.data);
    require(success, "Delegatecall failed");
    assembly { return(add(result, 32), mload(result)) }
  }

  receive() external payable {}
}
Study the fallback function carefully: it forwards arbitrary calls and returns implementation results. Note where upgrade and admin controls live.

screens.title: Storage Layout and Storage Collision
screens.narratorSegment: Storage collision is one of the most dangerous pitfalls in upgradeable contracts. Because implementation code runs on the proxy’s storage, the order and types of state variables declared by implementations must remain compatible across versions. Concretely, if version one declares uint256 value as the first variable and version two inserts a bool before value, the boolean will occupy the slot previously used for the uint256. That causes existing values to be misinterpreted or overwritten. In practice this leads to corrupted balances, broken flags, or worse. OpenZeppelin suggests a mitigation: reserve future slots by adding a reserved array named __gap at the end of upgradeable contracts so developers can introduce new variables without shifting critical existing slots. Another practical strategy is to use explicit storage libraries or single-slot storage patterns for metadata and admin pointers. A common misconception is assuming the compiler or deployment tooling will automatically reorder or migrate storage — it will not. Always review storage layouts when preparing an upgrade and run tooling that compares layouts. Testing upgrades on a local network and inspecting raw storage slots before and after an upgrade will reveal collisions early. The final question to keep in mind is: did I preserve slot indexing for every state variable the implementation touches?

keyIdea.title: Storage rule
keyIdea.text: Never change the order or types of existing state variables across implementations; use __gap to reserve slots for future additions.

content.html:
Definition

What is storage collision?

It occurs when a new implementation changes variable ordering, causing reads and writes to map to the wrong storage slots in the proxy.

Example variable ordering
// V1
uint256 public x;
bool public flag;

// V2 (incorrect)
bool public flag;
uint256 public x; // now maps to a different storage slot
Mitigations
  • Use a reserved __gap array to keep slots available for future variables.
  • Keep a strict ordering policy and document slot usage per version.
  • Use OpenZeppelin’s storage layout checks and upgrade testing tools before upgrading on mainnet.
Common mistake

Assuming adding a few variables is safe. Even small changes can shift slots and corrupt critical data. Always check layout compatibility.

screens.title: Initialization Pattern and Initializers
screens.narratorSegment: When you deploy an implementation contract, its constructor runs for that implementation contract’s address, not for the proxy. Because delegatecall executes implementation code in the proxy’s context, constructors on the implementation are not executed on the proxy. This is why upgradeable contracts use initializer functions that are called through the proxy after deployment. An initializer typically sets up ownership, token name and symbol, or other initial state. To avoid multiple initialization calls, use initializer modifiers from a library such as OpenZeppelin’s Initializable, which ensures the function runs only once. The safe process looks like this: deploy implementation, deploy proxy pointing to implementation, call initialize on the proxy, verify that state is set, then restrict initialize so it cannot be called again. A common error is calling initialize directly on the implementation address — that sets state in the implementation, not in the proxy. Another pitfall is forgetting to run initialize after upgrading to a new implementation that requires new initialization steps; in such cases use reinitializer logic with versioning to allow controlled additional initialization while preventing repeated or accidental runs. Always test the initializer path and confirm that the proxy’s storage contains expected values after initialization.

An initializer typically sets up ownership, token name and symbol, or other initial state. To avoid multiple initialization calls, use initializer modifiers from a library such as OpenZeppelin’s Initializable, which ensures the function runs only once. The safe process looks like this: deploy implementation, deploy proxy pointing to implementation, call initialize on the proxy, verify that state is set, then restrict initialize so it cannot be called again. A common error is calling initialize directly on the implementation address — that sets state in the implementation, not in the proxy. Another pitfall is forgetting to run initialize after upgrading to a new implementation that requires new initialization steps; in such cases use reinitializer logic with versioning to allow controlled additional initialization while preventing repeated or accidental runs. Always test the initializer path and confirm that the proxy’s storage contains expected values after initialization.

keyIdea.title: Initializer rule
keyIdea.text: Always call an initializer through the proxy exactly once; use Initializable to prevent multiple invocations and reinitialize with versioning when needed.

content.html:
Process Flow

Initialization steps

  1. Deploy implementation contract (constructor runs here).
  2. Deploy proxy pointing to implementation address.
  3. Call initializer on the proxy to set state in proxy storage.
  4. Lock initializer with Initializable modifiers to avoid multiple runs.
Code pattern
function initialize(string memory name, string memory symbol) public initializer {
  __ERC20_init(name, symbol);
  __Ownable_init();
  __UUPSUpgradeable_init();
}
Gotcha
Constructors on implementation do not initialize proxy state. Always call initializer through proxy and protect it with initializer modifiers.
Pro tip

Use reinitializer with a version number only when adding new state in a patch so initialization remains controlled and auditable.

screens.title: Deploying and Upgrading a UUPS Token (Hands-on)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on flow uses OpenZeppelin Upgrades with Hardhat to deploy a UUPS proxy and later upgrade it. keyIdea.text: Deploy MyTokenV1 using upgrades.deployProxy(kind: 'uups'), call initialize through proxy, then upgrade with upgrades.upgradeProxy and verify unchanged proxy address and preserved state.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Deploy script (excerpt)
const { ethers, upgrades } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const MyTokenV1 = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyTokenV1");
  const myToken = await upgrades.deployProxy(MyTokenV1, ["MyUpgradeableToken", "MUT"], {
    kind: "uups",
    initializer: "initialize"
  });
  await myToken.deployed();
  console.log("MyTokenV1 deployed to:", myToken.address);
}

main();
Upgrade script (excerpt)
const { ethers, upgrades } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const proxyAddress = "YOUR_PROXY_ADDRESS";
  const MyTokenV2 = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyTokenV2");
  const upgraded = await upgrades.upgradeProxy(proxyAddress, MyTokenV2);
  console.log("MyToken upgraded to V2 at:", upgraded.address);
}

main();
After upgrading, call getVersion() on the proxy and test new functions like burn to confirm behavior while balances persist.

fullNarratorScript:
Smart contracts on Ethereum are immutable by design. That immutability gives strong guarantees, but it also raises a practical problem: real software needs fixes and new features. In this lesson you’ll learn why upgradeable contracts exist, how the EVM opcode delegatecall makes them possible, and two widely used proxy patterns — Transparent Proxy and UUPS. You’ll also see a full code walkthrough of a simple proxy plus a practical upgrade flow using OpenZeppelin’s UUPS plugins. By the end you will be able to explain how a proxy preserves state while swapping implementation logic, why storage layout matters, how an initializer replaces a constructor, and where common pitfalls lie. A concrete example in this chapter shows deploying a token using UUPS, then upgrading it to add a burn function while keeping balances intact. Keep in mind a common misconception: upgradeability does not remove immutability of on-chain history, it simply separates state and logic so logic can evolve. As you proceed, notice how delegatecall preserves msg. sender, msg. value, and the proxy’s storage — that is the core insight that enables safe, stateful upgrades.

By the end of this chapter you will explain why immutable smart contract code creates practical problems for long-lived decentralized applications. You will distinguish major proxy patterns and describe who holds upgrade authority in Transparent Proxy versus UUPS. You will implement an upgradeable contract using the UUPS pattern with OpenZeppelin tooling and a local Hardhat network. Finally, you will identify and mitigate common risks like storage collisions and missing initializer calls. Each objective focuses on a different skill: conceptual understanding, pattern comparison, hands-on deployment, and safety practices. For example, after the implementation objective you will be able to deploy a token via an upgradeable proxy, call its initializer exactly once, then perform a controlled upgrade to a new implementation that adds a burn function while preserving balances. A common misconception is thinking upgrades magically migrate storage — they do not; the proxy’s storage layout must remain compatible. These objectives map to Learn, Understand, Apply, and Master: you will move from knowing the problem to safely performing and testing upgrades in a development environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on how you will practice upgrades and verify safety. You will run a local Hardhat deployment, observe proxy and implementation addresses, and run an upgrade script that preserves balances. The hands-on task uses OpenZeppelin Upgrades plugins to reduce manual error, but you must still inspect storage layout and call initializers correctly. For example, when you deploy MyTokenV1 via a UUPS proxy and later upgrade to MyTokenV2, you will check that getVersion now returns the updated version string and that existing token balances remain. Testing includes simulating upgrades and explicitly checking storage slots where variables live. A common misconception is assuming the implementation’s constructor runs during proxy deployment. It does not. Instead, you will call an initializer through the proxy exactly once, and you will protect it using initializer modifiers provided by OpenZeppelin. These practices let you demonstrate competence: deploy, initialize, upgrade, and verify state consistency and new functionality without migrating user data.

Ethereum smart contracts are immutable once deployed. That immutability means the bytecode at an address cannot be altered, which preserves trust. However, immutability also prevents bug fixes and feature additions in the deployed code. Imagine a token contract with a bug in its transfer logic discovered after months of use. Redeploying a new contract would mean migrating all balances and convincing users to move to a new address — a costly and error-prone process. Upgradeable contracts solve this by separating state and logic: a proxy holds the state and user-facing address, while the logic lives in separate implementation contracts that the proxy can point to. The central claim is this: by using a forwarding mechanism that runs implementation code in the proxy’s storage, we can change behavior without changing state or address. A common misconception is thinking upgrades change historical transactions; they do not. The chain’s history remains intact. What changes is the active logic that handles new calls. The practical significance is large: projects can fix critical bugs, patch vulnerabilities, or add features while preserving on-chain data. Consider a simple token: with a proxy you can add a burn function later without moving balances. To make this safe, we must understand how forwarding works and what can go wrong with storage layout.

delegatecall is the EVM opcode that makes proxy-based upgrades possible. Unlike a normal external call which uses the callee’s storage and context, delegatecall executes the code of a target contract while keeping the storage, msg. sender, and msg. value of the calling contract. Practically, this means the proxy forwards the calldata to the implementation and executes that implementation's code against the proxy’s storage layout. A clear example: if an implementation’s increment function increments a storage slot named value, using delegatecall causes that slot in the proxy to change. A common misconception is treating delegatecall like a message that simply runs code elsewhere; instead it effectively borrows the implementation’s code and operates directly on the proxy’s state. This behavior is powerful but dangerous: bugs in implementation code write directly into the proxy's storage. Because delegatecall preserves msg. sender, access control checks in the implementation will see the original caller rather than the proxy, which is usually desired. When designing proxies, always ensure the proxy correctly forwards calls and returns data and that the implementation functions are written with the assumption they operate on the proxy state. As you move to code examples, keep this operational model in mind — it explains storage collisions and why initializers must be called through the proxy.

A proxy is minimal by design: it holds state variables and a pointer to the current implementation address, and it forwards all external calls to that implementation via delegatecall. The implementation contract contains business logic and assumes storage exists in the calling context. This separation gives two distinct responsibilities. The proxy is responsible for state persistence and upgradeability mechanics — storing the implementation pointer and enforcing who can change it. The implementation focuses on behavior: token transfers, business rules, and access checks. This division has consequences. For example, any storage layout declared in the implementation must match what the proxy expects at the same slots. Also, access control in the implementation should operate against msg. sender as seen through delegatecall, which means the implementation can enforce permissions that reference the original caller. The Transparent Proxy pattern adds admin handling in the proxy itself, allowing the admin to make management calls that are not forwarded. UUPS moves upgrade authorization into the implementation. When designing your system, think of the proxy as a stable envelope for evolving logic. A helpful analogy is a building with fixed wiring (state) and replaceable appliances (logic): you swap appliances without rewiring the house. What can go wrong? If upgrade authority is misconfigured or storage layouts differ between versions, you risk breaking the contract and corrupting user data.

Two prominent proxy patterns are the Transparent Proxy and UUPS. The Transparent Proxy places upgrade logic in the proxy contract itself and distinguishes calls from the admin and regular users. If the caller is the admin and the function matches a proxy-defined admin function, the proxy performs management actions; otherwise it delegatecalls to the implementation. This avoids accidental interception of admin functions by users, but introduces a limitation: the admin cannot call implementation functions that share signatures with the proxy. UUPS moves the upgrade logic into the implementation. The proxy becomes minimal — it only forwards calls and stores the implementation pointer. The implementation exposes functions like _authorizeUpgrade, and upgrade execution happens within the implementation contract. UUPS is more gas-efficient because the proxy is small, and it avoids the Transparent Proxy's signature clash. However, UUPS requires that every new implementation includes proper upgrade hooks; forgetting to include them makes the contract un-upgradeable. A practical contrast: Transparent Proxy centralizes upgrade authority into the proxy, which can be simpler to reason about in some governance models, while UUPS gives implementations control and relies on developer discipline. Which you choose depends on desired gas profile, governance model, and whether you want upgrade checks centralized or bundled with logic.

Looking at a minimal proxy example helps cement how forwarding and upgrade work. In the example proxy, the contract stores an implementation address and an admin address. An upgradeTo function lets the admin set a new implementation address with an authorization check. The fallback function uses delegatecall with the incoming msg. data, then returns the implementation result using inline assembly. This pattern means functions not defined on the proxy will be handled by delegatecall and executed against the proxy’s storage. The important operational detail is that the implementation’s constructor is never run in proxy context. Instead, state initialization must happen through an initializer function called via the proxy after deployment. A misconception to avoid: calling initialize on the implementation contract directly will set values in the implementation’s storage, not the proxy’s. Always call initialize through the proxy address. The code walkthrough in the content shows both a simple implementation contract with a value variable and the MyProxy contract with upgrade and fallback logic. Read the code to see where delegatecall is used and where admin checks guard upgrades. After you review the code, consider how you would add a reentrancy guard or access control while preserving storage layout.

Storage collision is one of the most dangerous pitfalls in upgradeable contracts. Because implementation code runs on the proxy’s storage, the order and types of state variables declared by implementations must remain compatible across versions. Concretely, if version one declares uint256 value as the first variable and version two inserts a bool before value, the boolean will occupy the slot previously used for the uint256. That causes existing values to be misinterpreted or overwritten. In practice this leads to corrupted balances, broken flags, or worse. OpenZeppelin suggests a mitigation: reserve future slots by adding a reserved array named __gap at the end of upgradeable contracts so developers can introduce new variables without shifting critical existing slots. Another practical strategy is to use explicit storage libraries or single-slot storage patterns for metadata and admin pointers. A common misconception is assuming the compiler or deployment tooling will automatically reorder or migrate storage — it will not. Always review storage layouts when preparing an upgrade and run tooling that compares layouts. Testing upgrades on a local network and inspecting raw storage slots before and after an upgrade will reveal collisions early. The final question to keep in mind is: did I preserve slot indexing for every state variable the implementation touches?

When you deploy an implementation contract, its constructor runs for that implementation contract’s address, not for the proxy. Because delegatecall executes implementation code in the proxy’s context, constructors on the implementation are not executed on the proxy. This is why upgradeable contracts use initializer functions that are called through the proxy after deployment. An initializer typically sets up ownership, token name and symbol, or other initial state. To avoid multiple initialization calls, use initializer modifiers from a library such as OpenZeppelin’s Initializable, which ensures the function runs only once. The safe process looks like this: deploy implementation, deploy proxy pointing to implementation, call initialize on the proxy, verify that state is set, then restrict initialize so it cannot be called again. A common error is calling initialize directly on the implementation address — that sets state in the implementation, not in the proxy. Another pitfall is forgetting to run initialize after upgrading to a new implementation that requires new initialization steps; in such cases use reinitializer logic with versioning to allow controlled additional initialization while preventing repeated or accidental runs. Always test the initializer path and confirm that the proxy’s storage contains expected values after initialization.
